title: Natural selection tends to oppose rather than generate complexity

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Natural selection tends to oppose rather than generate complexity

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Darwinian natural selection does not clearly imply the generation of complexity and in many respects tends to oppose it; a different mechanism, the intrinsic complexity of simple programs, is responsible for most great complexity in biology.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I will argue in this book that in many respects it tends to oppose complexity.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 1, “The Foundations for a New Kind of Science”; section “Some Past Initiatives” (from p. 12), p. 14. Scope: biological evolution and the origin of biological complexity

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch01-13: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.40

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing genomic and phylogenetic data can test restricted associations between selection and specified complexity measures. They cannot cleanly resolve the broad causal partition or the assertion that intrinsic program behavior explains most biological complexity.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define biological complexity metrics and estimate their changes under measured selection across phylogenies, experiments, and genomic time series. Compare selection-based models with intrinsic program-complexity models using out-of-sample causal predictions.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Biological complexity has no single accepted metric.

Selection, drift, development, and environment are strongly confounded.

Most great complexity is a scope-wide causal attribution.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.35
data existence: 0.65
operationalizability: 0.35
analysis feasibility: 0.3

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Genome archives and digital-evolution software let a team estimate some complexity trends with and without selection. Both are partial proxies: genomes are not a direct complexity measure, and Avida is not wild biology. Selection and complexity are statistically confounded in comparative data, so existing resources can challenge extreme versions and cannot show what produces most biological complexity.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure a declared complexity statistic along lineages with estimated selection intensity, in organisms and in digital evolution, and test the sign of the association. The claim is supported if complexity falls or stalls where selection is effective and rises where simple-program dynamics run without selection. It is refuted if selection systematically increases that statistic after the program-intrinsic contribution is controlled for.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Genome size and morphological disparity are contested proxies for complexity.

Selection intensity is usually inferred from the same traits whose complexity is at issue.

Digital evolution tests an abstract analogue, not most biological complexity.
